topics.title: Collatz Conjecture Generalizations
topics.text:
So some of you may have heard of Collatz Conjecture:



Start with any number $n$. Then, \begin{align*} n \to 3n+1 & \text{ if n is odd} \\ n \to \frac{n}{2} & \text{ if n is even} \end{align*}

Collatz Conjecture states that no matter what $n$ is, the above formula will result in $1$.



Here are a few things I noticed:



First off, why $3n+1$? Why not $5n+7$ or any general formula of the form $(2x-1)\cdot n + (2y-1)$ (The goal of the expression to change the odd number is to convert it to an even number, thus the odd coefficients) And furthermore, how will we know if an expression works or not if the sequence goes on for a long time?



For a more articulate description of this problem go to http://mathworld.wolfram.com/CollatzProblem.html



Well, I noticed that we will $always$ reach 1 if we reach a power of 2 (since it is even and we will keep dividing by 2 until we reach $2^0$).



As for seeing how things pan out if we replace $3n + 1$ with $xn + y$, if we ever reach a number we have seen before, we are stuck in an infinite loop, and will never reach 1.



One example of this:



Say we adopt $5n + 3$ instead of $3n + 1$, and choose our $n$ to be 3. Then, $5\cdot 3 + 3 = 18, \frac{18}{2} = 9, 9\cdot 5 + 3 = 48$, and since 48 is a multiple of $2^4$, we can take that out. We are left now with $\frac{48}{16} = 3$, which is the number we started with! Thus 1 can never be reached and we have proved this doesn't work.



Please let me know what you think of this interesting problem. If you have noticed or thought of explorations of this problem please reply/comment.

topics.title: Proof Theory?
topics.text:
So I was daydreaming one day and came to this weird conclusion.



Suppose that I have a true statement P. It doesn't matter whether mankind accepts P as true, just that P is true, but mankind doesn't know it is yet. Now how do we show mankind P is true? We prove it of course!



Let Q be the VALID proof that P is true. Now let R be the proof that Q exists. Now, mankind doesn't physically need to see Q in order to accept P is true. If mankind accepts R, then they accept Q exists, and since Q exists, P must be true, otherwise Q would not exist.



Now, mankind doesn't need to physically see R. All mankind needs to see is S, where S shows that R exists. BUT WAIT! Mankind doesn't even need to see that! Take T! T shows that S exists, then U, then V, ad infinitum.



So there are infinite "proofs" of true statements.



Here's where it gets even stranger. Since if R exists, P is true, then R must be a proof of P. Since Q is a proof of P, R=Q could be a possible end. So if R=Q, and by construction, R could be Q, then all R has to do to prove P is to prove R exists! So any statement proving itself exists would prove every single true statement at the same time!



Just a little something next time your math teacher asks you to prove Fermat's Last Theorem...

topics.title: Counting past infinity
topics.text:
I saw a cool vsauce video, so I thought I would put the stuff on here.



First of all, a little on cardinality. If I have 4 bananas, the cardinality of the set of bananas is 4. Simple. Natural numbers are also called cardinal numbers.



The set of all natural numbers is alpha null ( I think that's how you spell it). Obviously, alpha null has infinite elements.



What if I take a set of bananas with cardinality alpha null and label each one with a natural number. Obviously, every banana would have a number, since this set of bananas and the set of natural numbers have the same cardinality: alpha null.



If I add one banana to the set, I still have alpha null bananas. Same thing if I subtract one banana. Even if I add another alpha null bananas, I'll still have alpha null bananas. Infinity is weird that way.



But what if I wanted to label the bananas in the order I got them in? If I had alpha null bananas and than added one banana, what would I call the extra banana? The label would have to be a number bigger than alpha null, or bigger than this type of infinity.



The extra banana would be called omega, an ordinal number. Ordinal numbers aren't used to add or subtract from infinity. As I said earlier, adding one banana to alpha null bananas is still alpha null bananas. Ordinal numbers just label things.



So, if I have two sets of alpha null lines, I could label 1 set with the natural numbers and the other set with omega, omega + 1, omega + 2, etc.



And eventually, we reach omega times 2, omega times 3, up to omega times omega. However, this is just omega squared. Then comes omega cubed, then omega to the fourth, etc.



When we reach omega to the omega to the omega to the omega....(going on forever), it seems like we can't continue. But we can. This number is Epsilon naught. We can go on from there.



Now, how can we construct new ordinal numbers like omega + 1? Through the axiom of replacement. Here, we see that if we replace a set of, say, 5 bananas with 5 apples, we still have a set. This is useful.



So, if we have a set of alpha null things up to omega, we can replace each number with omega + x, where x is a number in the first set of alpha null things.



Now, a little bit on order type of a set. The order type of a set is the first ordinal number not needed to label the things in the set. For cardinal numbers, order type = cardinality. The order type of alpha null is omega. So, if a set is well ordered, as in every part of the set contains a beginning element, than the set describes a new ordinal number.



Moving back to epsilon naught, we can see that all these ordinal numbers have an order type, as they are well ordered. This order type must be bigger than all these ordinals. This is called Omega 1.



The cardinality of omega 1 is alpha 1. This means that this ordinal has to describe more things than the last alpha. If it didn't, it would be part of that set.



Using the axiom of replacement, we can continue jumping to higher ordinals. Omega 2, Omega 3, even Omega Omega. In fact, we can go up to omega omega omega omega....., where there are alpha null omegas describing the ordinal.



Now, we could keep going with replacement, even if we had no way to write the numbers.



On a side note, a little bit about axioms. An axiom is a definition. An assumption. We can create axioms. We assume axioms are true so math can make sense. So, why not make an axiom that there is a number so big that you can't reach it, no matter how many times you use replacement.



This is called an inaccessible cardinal. And we have already seen one. Alpha null.



Every number below alpha null is finite. No matter how you add, subtract, multiply, divide, or exponentiate finite numbers, you cannot reach an infinite like alpha null.



So, jumping from alpha null to the next inaccessible is like jumping from 0 to alpha null. Cool!



Theorists have made axioms describing infinite bigger than inaccessible as well. It goes on and on. It's infinity, after all.



Thanks if you made it this far :P! Make sure you check out VSauce's video on this, "How to count past infinity", which is where I got this info from.

topics.title: The Number Circle
topics.text:
Okay, lets take a step back for a moment. I don't care how far your education in mathematics goes, one thing that has never changed in your entire mathematical career is the idea of the number line: that is, that cardinal numbers come one after another on the scale: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so on.

That's about to change.

Now imagine taking the two ends of the number line and pulling them together into a number circle Of course, since the line is infinite, you'll clearly have to shrink the line, especially when I tell you that the number circle has a radius of 1 unit. Clearly, this number circle has some interesting properties. The easiest and simplest property is that infinity equals negative infinity. therefore, we can now define infinity: for simplicity's sake we'll call it as alpha. alpha equals negative alpha. Now, try to determine where 1 is on the number circle: as it turns out, the point marking 1 is the same point as the one marking zero: that is, 1=0. Trying a couple other numbers gives us a surprising result: any finite number equals zero. So, we'll really have to work with just alpha as our basic unit: the finite numbers are too small. If we go halfway between zero and infinity, we get alpha divided by two, a quarter would be alpha divided by 4, and so on.

I'll finish this intriguing post by saying that the so-called Cartesian plane is now a Cartesian sphere. Try draw some graphs: both in terms of alpha and not in terms of alpha. See what you find. Maybe there's more to be explored in this new direction, maybe not.
